stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.numerator: nodes where all 3 models returned grounded==true AND the LLM judge found semantic agreement
stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.basis: does NOT require citation verification or a clean adversarial check -- purely: did the 3 models derive the same rule from the cited text, independently.

citation_verification_rate.numerator: nodes where every cited source's quoted_text verified as a substring of the fetched page
citation_verification_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run (null/not computed if --skip-citation-check)
citation_verification_rate.basis: mechanical HTTP fetch + substring match, no model involved.

stage_b_parse_success_rate.numerator: nodes where the adversarial call returned parseable edge_cases (not truncated, not empty, no error) -- even after the round-23/24 retry
stage_b_parse_success_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
stage_b_parse_success_rate.basis: an infrastructure/reliability signal, not a gap-count -- a node can parse successfully and still expose real gaps, or fail to parse and expose none we know of.

full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.stage: all three stages combined -- this is the renamed former 'grounded_agreement_rate' (round 26; the old name was found to be mislabeled relative to its own definition, see docs/DEBT_PROJECT_ARCHITECTURE_SPEC.md S4's round-24 entry)
full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.basis: CLEAN-PASS = LLM-judged semantic agreement across all 3 grounded derivations AND all citations live-verified AND no adversarial gap found AND the adversarial check itself parsed successfully (round 26 -- a Stage B parse failure no longer silently reads as "no gaps", see spec S4). Numeric fingerprint is a secondary diagnostic only as of 2026-08-26 round 3, not part of this basis either.

grounded_agreement_rate.note: Deprecated alias for full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate (round 26), kept only so anything still reading this exact key doesn't break. This name was found to be mislabeled -- it was never actually a Stage-A-only measure despite the name. Use full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate (the honest name for the same number) or stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate (genuinely Stage-A-only) going forward.

scenario_pass_rate.stage: scenario level (depends on multiple nodes' CLEAN-PASS status)
scenario_pass_rate.numerator: concept-demo scenarios where every node_id they depend on is CLEAN-PASS this run
scenario_pass_rate.denominator: all concept-demo scenarios defined in the scenarios file
scenario_pass_rate.basis: a scenario passes iff every node_id it depends on is CLEAN-PASS in this same run

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer says the bank that issued her credit card (or the mortgage servicer collecting its own current loan) called her 9 times in six days about the past-due balance. No third-party collection agency is involved.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist never asks who the caller is. The 7-in-7 rule comes from Regulation F/FDCPA and binds only 'debt collectors'; original creditors and first-party servicers collecting their own non-defaulted debt are generally outside it (subject to state analogues). Applied as encoded, the node would tell this very common caller-type of consumer she has a presumptive federal violation when she likely has none.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's account was placed with Agency A, which called 4 times in a week, then re-placed with Agency B, which called 5 times the same week about the identical debt; the consumer reports 9 calls on one debt in seven days.
edge_cases.gap_description: The unit of count is per debt AND per debt collector; the encoding and checklist only ask about the debt, not which collector placed each call. Aggregating calls across two collectors yields a false 'presumptively unlawful' finding (and conversely could mask which single collector, if any, actually exceeded the cap).

edge_cases.scenario: A collector places 10 calls in five days about one debt; the consumer never picks up, and only 2 of the calls leave voicemails while the rest simply ring out or are declined.
edge_cases.gap_description: The encoded exclusion for 'calls not connected to the dialed number' is undefined and invites treating unanswered/ring-out calls as excluded. Under the CFPB's commentary, a call that reaches the consumer's line counts even if unanswered or sent to voicemail; only calls that never connect (e.g., dropped by the carrier) are excluded. Misapplying it here flips a presumptive violation into a false 'compliant' answer in the most common fact pattern of all (consumer doesn't answer).

results.derivation_summary: Under 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a), a debt collector must, in the initial communication or within five days after it, send a written notice stating the amount of the debt, the name of the creditor owed, that the debt will be assumed valid unless the consumer disputes it within thirty days after receipt of the notice, that a written dispute within that period will require the collector to obtain and mail verification or a copy of a judgment, and that a written request within that period will require the collector to provide the name and address of the original creditor if different from the current creditor. Regulation F adds detail: 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(a)(1) allows the information to be given in the initial communication (in writing or orally) or by written notice within five days, and § 1006.34(c) itemizes the required validation information (the collector-communication disclosure; debt information including collector and consumer names/addresses, current creditor, itemization date and amounts, and current amount; consumer-protection information including the dispute-window end date, assumption-of-validity statement, original-creditor request right, and CFPB website statement; and consumer-response prompts and mailing addresses). As to timing, § 1006.34(b)(5) defines the 'validation period' as beginning when the collector provides the validation information and ending 30 days after the consumer receives or is assumed to receive it, and the collector may assume receipt on any date at least five days (excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays, and Sundays) after it provides the information — so the clock runs from receipt, not mailing. During that period, under 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b), otherwise-lawful collection may continue unless the consumer disputes in writing, in which case collection must cease until verification, a judgment copy, or the original creditor's name and address is mailed to the consumer.

edge_cases.gap_description: Neither the logic nor the checklist encodes 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(d), which provides that a formal pleading in a civil action is NOT an 'initial communication.' Applied as encoded, the rule would treat service of the complaint as the triggering initial communication, wrongly flag a §1692g violation for the missing 5-day notice, and wrongly compute (and close) the 30-day dispute window from the service date rather than from the first non-pleading communication. Suit-first collection by debt buyers is very common.

edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist never asks the threshold status question — whether the collecting entity is a 'debt collector' under § 1692a(6) (or a covered person under Reg F) as opposed to a creditor collecting its own debts in its own name. edge_cases.scenario: The collector mailed the validation notice to a stale address obtained from a skip trace; the envelope was returned as undeliverable and the consumer first learned of the debt months later from a credit report. results.derivation_summary: Under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a), an action on a contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument must be brought within four years (with a special three-month limit for deficiency-type money judgments after a trustee's sale under a deed of trust or mortgage, and an exception under Section 336a). Section 337(d) adds that once that period has run, a person may not sue, arbitrate, or otherwise initiate legal proceedings to collect the debt, and the period can be extended only under Section 360. Section 360 allows the clock to be restarted only by a written, signed acknowledgment or promise, or by a payment of principal or interest (which tolls/restarts from the time of each payment), but expressly provides that no payment by itself revives a cause of action that is already barred. If the claim arose in another state or country and is time-barred there, § 361 bars suit in California as well, except in favor of a California citizen who held the claim from accrual.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a credit card in March 2019 and is served in September 2023 with a collection complaint; she asks whether the suit was time-barred because it was filed more than four years after her last payment. The four-year period would have run in March 2023 but for California Emergency Rule of Court 9, which tolled all civil statutes of limitations over 180 days from April 6, 2020 to October 1, 2020 (178 days).
edge_cases.gap_description: The node applies a flat accrual-plus-4-years computation and treats tolling only as a fact-dependent item the consumer must volunteer ('any facts suggesting tolling, e.g., debtor's absence from the state'). Emergency Rule 9's 178-day COVID tolling is automatic and universal, not something a consumer would ever report as a 'fact,' yet it is outcome-determinative for the very large cohort of California consumer debts that defaulted roughly 2016-2020. The node would tell a consumer the suit is time-barred when it is in fact timely by up to 178 days, inviting her to rely on a losing defense.

edge_cases.scenario: A borrower stopped paying a defaulted federal Direct/FFEL student loan in 2015 and, in 2026, receives a collection suit or administrative wage-garnishment notice; he asks whether the four-year California SOL bars collection. He also has a defaulted private student loan from the same period.
edge_cases.gap_description: Neither the logic nor the checklist screens for the identity/type of the obligation as a federally guaranteed or federally held student loan. 20 U.S.C. § 1091a abolishes all limitations periods for actions to collect federal student loans and expressly preempts state SOLs; similar federal rules govern other government-backed consumer debts. The node would confidently declare an eleven-year-old federal student loan 'expired' and tell the borrower a creditor is statutorily barred from even initiating collection — a flatly wrong and potentially very costly answer — while the same analysis is correct for the private loan, so the consumer has no cue that the distinction matters.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer received a Chapter 7 discharge in 2023 covering a credit-card balance he defaulted on in 2021; in 2026 a debt buyer sues him on that account. He asks whether the four-year SOL is a defense.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist's generic 'other statutory tolling' item does not surface bankruptcy, which cuts both ways and is common among consumer-debt defendants: 11 U.S.C. § 108(c) plus the automatic stay extends the limitations period for the pendency of the case, so the node's flat computation can wrongly declare a claim time-barred; and more importantly a discharge is a complete substantive bar, so the node's 'not expired' output would misleadingly imply the consumer is exposed on a debt that cannot lawfully be collected at all. The node needs a bankruptcy screening item rather than folding bankruptcy into unresolved 'tolling.'
